title: Is every answer of an expression even, whatever number we put in?
description: The expression four m plus two q is shown to be always even by taking out the factor two, and then tried with m as four and q as minus nine. Then x squared plus two is tested with x as six and as three. Keeko raises the doubt that one even answer shows an expression is always even.
teaching_notes: One idea: an expression is always even when the factor two can be taken out of it, and one failing example is enough to show it is not always even. Watch for students who trust an expression after one or two examples that work.

source: Show that 4m + 2q is always even and try it with m = 4, q =
video_script.why: A learner shows an expression is always even by taking out the factor two, and shows another is not always even with one example.
video_script.substitution: the book's own expressions: four m plus two q, and x squared plus two
video_script.anchor: the expressions 4m + 2q and x² + 2 on the board, with number cards put in for the letters, as in the book
video_script.wrong_answer: x squared plus two is always even because it worked for six
video_script.wrong_move: thinks one even answer is enough to show an expression is always even
video_script.payoff_line: Four m plus two q is always even. But x squared plus two is even only when x is even.

final_answer.value: 4m + 2q is always even; x² + 2 is even only when x is even
final_answer.spoken: four m plus two q is always even, but x squared plus two is even only when x is even

hold_back: 4m + 2q is always even; x² + 2 is even only when x is even
maths_rules: 4m + 2q = 2 x 2m + 2 x q = 2(2m + q), so 2 is a factor for any whole numbers m and q
x = 3: 3^2 = 9, 9 + 2 = 11, odd, so x^2 + 2 is not always even
x even: x^2 even, plus 2 even; x odd: x^2 odd, plus 2 odd
video_script.design: One idea: take out the factor two to show always even, and use one failing example to show not always. Assumes even numbers have the factor two and substitution into an expression. Wrong idea: one example that works is enough. The two expressions stay on the board while values are put in.

marks.ask: a question mark glows over each expression

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about two expressions with letters in them.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Whatever whole numbers we put in for the letters, is the answer always even?

beats.on_screen: the two expressions stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: an even number split as 2 × something; an expression is always even when it is even for every whole number put in

marks.even: dots for six sit in three pairs and are written as two times three
marks.always: the words always even are written, with every whole number sliding into the slot

narration: <bookmark mark='even'/>An even number has two as a factor. Six is two times three.
<bookmark mark='always'/>An expression is always even when it is even for every whole number we put in.

beats.on_screen: Given: 4m + 2q, with m = 4 and q = −9; and x² + 2, with x = 6 and x = 3

marks.given: the two expressions and the values are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the expressions are four m plus two q, and x squared plus two.

beats.on_screen: To find: is each expression always even?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find whether each expression is always even.

marks.split: four m and two q are each written with a factor two
marks.take: the factor two is taken out in front of a bracket

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step one, take out the common factor. Four m is two times two m, and two q is two times q.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Both parts have the factor two. Four m plus two q is two times the bracket two m plus q. That makes it always even.

marks.put: four goes into m and minus nine goes into q
marks.sum: sixteen and minus eighteen add to minus two

narration: <bookmark mark='put'/>Step two, try m as four and q as minus nine. Four times four is sixteen, and two times minus nine is minus eighteen.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Sixteen plus minus eighteen is minus two, which is even.

marks.add: thirty six plus two shows thirty eight

narration: <bookmark mark='square'/>Step three, try x as six. Six squared is thirty six.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Thirty six plus two is thirty eight, which is even.

beats.on_screen: x = 3: 3² = 9; 9 + 2 = 11, odd. So x² + 2 is not always even

marks.add: nine plus two shows eleven and it is tagged odd

narration: <bookmark mark='square'/>Step four, try x as three. Three squared is nine.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Nine plus two is eleven, which is odd. One odd answer is enough to show x squared plus two is not always even.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 4m + 2q is always even; x² + 2 is even only when x is even
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Four m plus two q is always even. But x squared plus two is even only when x is even.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the two expressions
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows x² + 2 always even because x = 6 gave 38, struck through; x = 3 gives 11 beside it

marks.doubt: the bubble with the claim appears
marks.three: the card x equals three gives eleven beside it

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks x squared plus two is always even because it worked for six.
<bookmark mark='three'/>But always means for every number. When x is three, the answer is eleven, which is odd.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Many examples that work cannot prove always. One example that fails shows it is not always.
